title: Knowledge check — 8 questions
note: Unlocks after the applied activity is submitted. Retakes are free and unlimited.

questions.prompt: Why does a story lose to a model in a budget conversation, even when the story is more accurate?
options: Finance leaders are trained to distrust qualitative input
A model can be challenged, adjusted, and agreed — it converts a claim into a form comparable against competing claims on the same money
Stories take longer to present than models
Models are more likely to be correct than practitioner judgment
questions.explanation: Being arguable is the property that matters. A story can only be believed or not, and belief is a weak instrument against a spreadsheet. D is explicitly not the claim — the story is often more accurate.

questions.prompt: Your attrition model gets challenged on the replacement-cost multiplier you used. What has actually happened?
options: The model failed and should be rebuilt with defensible inputs
Finance is signalling they won't fund the request
The shape of your reasoning was accepted and only the parameters are in dispute — which is the conversation you wanted
You presented with too much precision and invited scrutiny
questions.explanation: Getting to a parameter argument means the model was taken seriously. That stage doesn't exist for a story, which is the entire point of bringing one.

questions.prompt: In a regretted-attrition model, which input typically carries the most weight and receives the least scrutiny?
options: Recruitment agency fees
Interviewer and hiring manager time
Onboarding and training cost
The productivity ramp — months until a replacement reaches the departed person's output
questions.explanation: For complex roles it often exceeds everything else combined, and most published per-hire figures omit it entirely. Which means a model that includes it explicitly is more defensible than one citing a headline industry number.

questions.prompt: Why is the "regretted" flag in your HRIS specifically unreliable? `[V]`
options: It's usually left blank by default
It's set by whoever closed the requisition — sometimes the manager who caused the departure, recording a judgment under pressure as an interested party
Different HRIS vendors define it differently
It's a lagging indicator that only updates quarterly
questions.explanation: A judgment field populated by a party with an interest in the answer — and every attrition model in the organization rests on it. Knowing this about your own systems is the contribution an HRBP makes that neither analytics nor Finance can.

questions.prompt: Three of six people have left a team in a year. What does the module recommend?
options: Report it as 50% attrition, which is the accurate rate
Exclude the team from analysis, since the population is too small
State "three of six," volunteer the coincidence test before being asked, and argue direction and mechanism rather than magnitude
Combine it with similar teams to reach a defensible sample
questions.explanation: "50% attrition" is arithmetically identical and rhetorically dishonest, because percentages imply a supporting population. Volunteering the limitation is the strongest credibility move available and costs nothing — everyone competent already knows.

questions.prompt: What does the module mean by "confident garbage in front of a CFO is worse than no model at all"?
options: CFOs prefer qualitative arguments from HR partners
A missing number costs one conversation; a wrong number that gets repeated and then corrected by someone else costs the next five
Financial models require certification that HR business partners don't hold
AI-assisted models are inherently less reliable than manual ones
questions.explanation: The asymmetry is about credibility over time, not about any single meeting. D misstates it — the danger isn't AI assistance, it's AI assistance on inputs that don't mean what the model assumes.

questions.prompt: Where should AI be used in building these models, and where not?
options: For the inputs, since it can access market benchmark data
Nowhere — financial modelling requires human construction throughout
For structure, forgotten variables, and sensitivity tables; not for supplying the numbers, which come from your systems with recorded provenance
For the final narrative only, after the model is complete
questions.explanation: Skeleton-building is genuinely what it's good at; input-supply is where the foundation problem bites. A is the specific trap — invented benchmarks are confident, plausible, and exactly what Module 3's teardown exists to catch.

questions.prompt: Why does the activity ask you to name your weakest assumption first?
options: To demonstrate humility to the reader

Because a hostile reader will find it anyway, and naming it first converts an attack into a stated limitation — and a case that fails its own sensitivity test, reported honestly, is worth more than one that passes untested
Because sensitivity analysis is required in financial submissions
To reduce the number of questions asked in the meeting
questions.explanation: It's a strength move, not a concession: you keep control of the framing and you learn whether your conclusion is robust. A submission that discovers its case doesn't survive is a success for this module.
